description: Trailing comma after last field in JSON object
adversary_notes: Payload: {"tool":"Bash","args":{"command":"ls"},} — trailing comma is invalid JSON but accepted by JS engines and some lenient parsers; tests strict RFC 8259 compliance

description: Missing opening brace — JSON starts mid-object
adversary_notes: Payload: "tool":"Bash","args":{}} — no opening brace; some streaming parsers may synchronize on first key and partially decode

description: Duplicate keys in request object — 'tool' appears twice
adversary_notes: Payload: {"tool":"Read","tool":"Bash","args":{}} — RFC 8259 says behavior is undefined for duplicate keys; some parsers take last value (Bash), others take first (Read), enabling tool confusion attacks

description: Unquoted numeric string where tool name string is expected
adversary_notes: Payload: {"tool":42,"args":{}} — integer where string expected; tests whether type validation happens at decode time or after

description: Single-quoted strings instead of double-quoted (Python dict literal style)
adversary_notes: Payload: {'tool':'Bash','args':{'command':'ls'}} — single quotes are not valid JSON; Python eval()-based parsers would accept this and are vulnerable to injection

description: Unescaped backslash in command string path
adversary_notes: Payload: {"command":"C:\path\to\evil"} with literal unescaped backslashes — invalid JSON escape sequence; tests whether parser rejects or silently drops the backslash

description: Literal unescaped newline embedded inside a JSON string value
adversary_notes: Payload contains actual 0x0A byte inside a JSON string (not \n escape) — RFC 8259 forbids literal control chars in strings; lenient parsers that accept it may misparse the length-prefixed framing

description: Missing value after key — bare key with colon and no value
adversary_notes: Payload: {"tool":,"args":{}} — colon followed immediately by comma; tests parser error recovery and whether partial parse state leaks

description: Extra closing brace after valid complete JSON object
adversary_notes: Payload: {"tool":"Bash","args":{"command":"ls"}}} — extra closing brace; streaming parsers that stop at first complete object will parse the valid part and ignore the tail, potentially processing an attacker-chosen request

description: JSON with comment syntax (// and /* */) which is not valid JSON
adversary_notes: Payload: {/* request */ "tool":"Bash", // execute this\n"args":{"command":"ls"}} — JSON5/JSONC comments; parsers that strip comments before parsing may have injection surface in the comment itself

description: args field as integer 42 instead of object
adversary_notes: Integer for args; if daemon checks args type lazily (only when accessing subfields), an integer may pass initial validation and panic on field access

description: args field as boolean false instead of object
adversary_notes: Boolean false for args; in Go, json.Unmarshal into map[string]interface{} would fail; into interface{} it succeeds as bool — tests which type the daemon uses for args container

description: args field as null
adversary_notes: Null args; Go json.Unmarshal sets pointer fields to nil on null — if daemon dereferences args.command without nil check, causes panic (DoS via nil deref)

description: args field as positional array instead of named object
adversary_notes: Array for args; some adapters accept positional args and map array[0] to 'command' — if so, attacker controls command by controlling first array element without using named key

description: authority_chain as a plain string 'none' instead of array
adversary_notes: String for authority_chain; if parser treats non-array as empty chain, attacker submits 'none' and gets zero-hop chain behavior — tests whether delegation layer validates chain type

description: authority_chain as an object instead of array
adversary_notes: Object for authority_chain; if parser accepts object-as-array by treating object values as elements, the fake token object may be treated as a delegation hop

description: session_id as integer 12345 instead of string
adversary_notes: Integer session_id; Go json.Unmarshal into string will fail but into interface{} succeeds as float64(12345) — tests whether session_id type is strictly validated at decode boundary

description: session_id as boolean false instead of string
adversary_notes: Boolean for session_id; if coerced to string 'false', may collide with another session named 'false'; if coerced to empty string, gets default session label

description: session_id as array ['session','1'] instead of string
adversary_notes: Array for session_id; some serializers join array elements with ',' making session_id='session,1'; tests whether array-as-string coercion creates exploitable session namespace

description: Entire CheckRequest as a JSON array instead of object
adversary_notes: Payload: [{"tool":"Bash","args":{"command":"ls"}}] — top-level array; if server reads first element and treats as request, the batch wrapper is silently stripped and the inner request executes

description: command string exactly 32KB — CEL expression depth limit probe
adversary_notes: 32KB command exactly at common CEL string evaluation limit; tests whether CEL evaluator enforces string size limit before or after parsing

description: command string exactly 32KB + 1 byte — one byte over CEL limit
adversary_notes: 32KB+1 command; off-by-one above limit; tests whether boundary check is < or <= (exclusive vs inclusive)

description: args JSON body exactly 2MB - 1 byte (just under wire limit)
adversary_notes: Just under 2MB wire limit; should be processed (though denied for other reasons) — tests whether near-limit requests are handled without corruption

description: args JSON body exactly 2MB + 1 byte (just over wire limit)
adversary_notes: One byte over 2MB wire limit; daemon must reject before parsing; tests whether length-prefix check is enforced before JSON decode (prevents memory exhaustion)

description: session_id exactly 1024 characters long
adversary_notes: 1024-byte session_id probes session map key allocation; if no limit is enforced, memory-mapped session stores may allocate 1KB per session for key storage

description: file_path exactly 4096 bytes (PATH_MAX on Linux)
adversary_notes: PATH_MAX = 4096 on Linux; file path at exact system limit tests whether daemon validates path length before passing to OS syscalls

description: file_path exactly 4097 bytes (one byte over PATH_MAX)
adversary_notes: One byte over PATH_MAX; OS syscall will return ENAMETOOLONG; tests whether daemon catches this before syscall or lets kernel reject it

description: Write content field with 1MB of repeated pattern data
adversary_notes: 1MB content field; tests whether SecretScan and CEL evaluation apply to large content blobs without OOM or timeout; repeated pattern avoids compression advantages

description: authority_chain with 100 delegation hops (well beyond 8-hop limit)
adversary_notes: 100-hop delegation chain far exceeds 8-hop limit; tests whether chain length check is O(1) guard at entry or O(n) validation that could be slow for very long chains

description: Deeply nested args object 200 levels deep
adversary_notes: Deeply nested JSON object; JSON parsers with recursive descent may stack overflow at high nesting depth; Go encoding/json has a 10000-level limit but CEL may have lower limits

description: UTF-8 BOM (EF BB BF) prepended before JSON object
adversary_notes: Wire payload starts with UTF-8 BOM bytes ï»¿ before the JSON; Go json.Decoder rejects BOM but some middleware strips it first, potentially allowing the request through

description: Zero-width space (U+200B) injected inside a JSON field name
adversary_notes: Payload: {"to​ol":"Bash"} — zero-width space inside field name makes it visually identical to "tool" but bytes differ; if parser normalizes Unicode field names, it may match the key and process the value

description: Zero-width non-joiner (U+200C) embedded in session_id value
adversary_notes: ZWNJ in session_id; if session store normalizes to NFC/NFKC before lookup, ZWNJ may be stripped and collide with session without the ZWNJ; enables session state hijack

description: Surrogate pair character in session_id (unpaired surrogate U+D800)
adversary_notes: Unpaired UTF-16 surrogate in session_id; � is not valid UTF-8; some JSON parsers accept WTF-8 (allowing surrogates) while others reject — tests codec strictness

description: Right-to-left override character (U+202E) in tool name field
adversary_notes: RTL override in tool name makes "Bash" display as "hsaB" in logs/UIs; string comparison with "Bash" may still match if comparison ignores control chars — tool name confusion for log evasion

description: Mixed script in file path: Latin + Cyrillic lookalikes + CJK
adversary_notes: Mixed Cyrillic and CJK chars in path; OS resolves paths byte-by-byte so non-ASCII paths are safe, but CEL string pattern matching with " /etc/* " may fail to catch non-ASCII path components

description: Overlong UTF-8 encoding of forward slash (0xC0 0xAF instead of 0x2F)
adversary_notes: Overlong encoding À¯ is an invalid UTF-8 representation of / (U+002F); strict parsers reject it, but systems that decode then check path may bypass /etc/ prefix rules if they decode before checking

description: Non-canonical UTF-8: three-byte encoding of ASCII character (e in etc)
adversary_notes: Fullwidth percent-sign (U+FF05) in path simulates non-canonical encoding tricks; if CEL checks path as string while OS resolves bytes, rule may check /％tc/shadow and miss the /etc/ pattern

description: Supplementary plane character (U+1F600 emoji) in command argument
adversary_notes: Supplementary-plane emoji embedded in path component; Go strings are byte sequences so len() != rune count; string slicing around the emoji may produce split surrogates and incorrect prefix matches

description: NULL-terminated-style string in file_path: path with embedded NUL then fake extension
adversary_notes: NUL byte mid-path: Go strings allow NUL but C libraries used by some file ops stop at NUL; CEL may see full string "/tmp/safe.txt�/etc/shadow" and match /tmp/* while OS open() sees only "/tmp/safe.txt"

description: Only tool field present, args completely absent
adversary_notes: No args field; if daemon defaults missing args to empty map {}, Bash tool with empty args may execute with no command — tests whether missing args triggers validation error or silent empty-command execution

description: Only args field present, tool field completely absent
adversary_notes: No tool field; if daemon defaults missing tool to empty string or a default tool, the command executes under an unintended tool adapter; tests required-field enforcement

description: Completely empty JSON object {} — all fields absent
adversary_notes: Empty object; all fields missing; daemon must return structured error without panicking on zero-value struct; zero-value Go struct has tool="", args=nil, session_id="" which may match default session state

description: All fields present but all set to empty or zero values
adversary_notes: Structurally complete but semantically empty; empty tool string and empty session_id test whether validator checks for empty-string vs missing field

description: tool and args present but session_id field absent
adversary_notes: Missing session_id; if daemon assigns a default session for missing IDs (e.g., empty string), all anonymous requests share the same session watermark — enabling cross-request state interference

description: Bash tool with Write-style args (file_path + content instead of command)
adversary_notes: Wrong args schema for tool: Write args sent to Bash adapter; if Bash adapter ignores unknown fields, it gets no command and executes empty; if it errors, tests adapter isolation

description: Bash args present but required command sub-field missing
adversary_notes: Args object present but command key missing; if daemon executes Bash with empty command string, result is shell with no input; tests required sub-field validation at adapter layer

description: Args with extra undocumented privilege-escalation field
adversary_notes: Extra undocumented fields that imply privilege escalation; if adapter uses a lenient deserializer that copies known fields and ignores unknown, the extra fields are silently dropped — but tests if any adapter acts on them

description: security_label present but as empty object {}
adversary_notes: Empty security_label object; all three numeric fields missing; Go JSON unmarshal into struct sets missing numeric fields to 0 — attacker gets {conf:0, int:0, cat:0} without explicitly setting them

description: authority_chain array with a null element: [null]
adversary_notes: authority_chain with null element; if delegation layer iterates chain and dereferences each hop without nil check, the null element causes a panic (DoS); or null hop may be treated as a valid zero-value delegation
